title: Aneurysm
description: Bulge in the wall of a blood vessel
wiki_lead: An aneurysm is an outward bulging, likened to a bubble or balloon, caused by a localized, abnormal, weak spot on a blood vessel wall. Aneurysms may be a result of a hereditary condition or an acquired disease. Aneurysms can also be a nidus (starting point) for clot formation (thrombosis) and embolization. As an aneurysm increases in size, the risk of rupture increases, which could lead to uncontrolled bleeding. Although they may occur in any blood vessel, particularly lethal examples include aneurysms of the circle of Willis in the brain, aortic aneurysms affecting the thoracic aorta, and abdominal aortic aneurysms. Aneurysms can arise in the heart following a heart attack, including both ventricular and atrial septal aneurysms. Congenital atrial septal aneurysms are a rare heart defect.
wiki_excerpt:
An aneurysm is an outward bulging, likened to a bubble or balloon, caused by a localized, abnormal, weak spot on a blood vessel wall. Aneurysms may be a result of a hereditary condition or an acquired disease. Aneurysms can also be a nidus (starting point) for clot formation (thrombosis) and embolization. As an aneurysm increases in size, the risk of rupture increases, which could lead to uncontrolled bleeding. Although they may occur in any blood vessel, particularly lethal examples include aneurysms of the circle of Willis in the brain, aortic aneurysms affecting the thoracic aorta, and abdominal aortic aneurysms. Aneurysms can arise in the heart following a heart attack, including both ventricular and atrial septal aneurysms. Congenital atrial septal aneurysms are a rare heart defect.


Etymology
The word is from Greek: ἀνεύρυσμα, aneurysma, "dilation", from ἀνευρύνειν, aneurynein, "to dilate".


Classification
Aneurysms are classified by type, morphology, or location.


True and false aneurysms
A true aneurysm is one that involves all three layers of the wall of an artery (intima, media and adventitia). True aneurysms include atherosclerotic, syphilitic, and congenital aneurysms, as well as ventricular aneurysms that follow transmural myocardial infarctions (aneurysms that involve all layers of the attenuated wall of the heart are also considered true aneurysms).
A false aneurysm, or pseudoaneurysm, is a collection of blood leaking completely out of an artery or vein but confined next to the vessel by the surrounding tissue. This blood-filled cavity will eventually either thrombose (clot) enough to seal the leak or rupture out of the surrounding tissue.
Pseudoaneurysms can be caused by trauma that punctures the artery, such as knife and bullet wounds, as a result of percutaneous surgical procedures such as coronary angiography or arterial grafting, or use of an artery for injection.


Morphology

Aneurysms can also be classified by their macroscopic shapes and sizes and are described as either saccular or fusiform. The shape of an aneurysm is not specific for a specific disease. The size of the base or neck is useful in determining the chance of for example endovascular coiling.
Saccular aneurysms, or "berry" aneurysms, are spherical in shape and involve only a portion of the vessel wall; they usually range from 5 to 20 cm (2.0 to 7.9 in) in diameter, and are often filled, either partially or fully, by a thrombus.Saccular aneurysms have a "neck" that connects the aneurysm to its main ("parent") artery, a larger, rounded area, called the dome.
Fusiform aneurysms ("spindle-shaped" aneurysms) are variable in both their diameter and length; their diameters can extend up to 20 cm (7.9 in). They often involve large portions of the ascending and transverse aortic arch, the abdominal aorta, or, less frequently, the iliac arteries.


Location
Aneurysms can also be classified by their location:

Arterial and venous, with arterial being more common.
The heart, including coronary artery aneurysms, ventricular aneurysms, aneurysm of sinus of Valsalva, and aneurysms following cardiac surgery.
The aorta, namely aortic aneurysms including thoracic aortic aneurysms and abdominal aortic aneurysms.
The brain, including cerebral aneurysms, berry aneurysms, and Charcot–Bouchard aneurysms.
The legs, including popliteal artery aneurysms.
The kidney, including renal artery aneurysms and intraparenchymal aneurysms.
Capillary aneurysms are flesh-colored solitary lesions, resembling an intradermal nevus, which may suddenly grow larger and darker and become blue-black or black as a result of thrombosis.
The large vessels such as external and internal jugular veins
Cerebral aneurysms, also known as intracranial or brain aneurysms, occur most commonly in the anterior cerebral artery, which is part of the circle of Willis. This can cause severe strokes leading to death. The next most common sites of cerebral aneurysm occurrence are in the internal carot
grok_lead: An aneurysm is a bulge or ballooning in the wall of a blood vessel resulting from a localized weakness in the vessel's structure, which can potentially rupture and cause severe internal bleeding or death. These abnormal dilations most commonly affect arteries, such as the aorta or cerebral vessels, and may develop gradually over years without initial symptoms. Aneurysms occur in approximately 1-2% of the population overall, with prevalence varying by type (e.g., ~3-5% for unruptured intracranial in adults and ~1% for abdominal aortic in those over 50), though only a small fraction rupture, making early detection and management critical to prevent complications like stroke or hemorrhagic shock. Aneurysms are classified by their location and shape, with the most prevalent types being aortic aneurysms (in the body's main artery) and cerebral aneurysms (in brain arteries). Aortic aneurysms are further divided into abdominal (affecting the lower aorta) and thoracic (in the chest portion), while cerebral ones are often saccular, resembling a berry-like outpouching. Less common sites include peripheral arteries in the legs or vessels in the spleen or kidneys. The risk of rupture increases with aneurysm size (particularly larger than 7 mm for cerebral types) and growth rate, and is highest for giant cerebral aneurysms exceeding 25 mm or those in high-flow areas. The exact causes of aneurysms are not always clear but often involve a combination of genetic predisposition and acquired factors that weaken arterial walls. High blood pressure, smoking, and atherosclerosis contribute by damaging vessel linings over time, while hereditary conditions like polycystic kidney disease or connective tissue disorders (e.g., Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) elevate risk. Other risk factors include age (most common between 30-60 years for cerebral aneurysms and after 65 for aortic), female sex (for cerebral aneurysms), family history, and trauma or infection. Preventive measures focus on controlling blood pressure, quitting tobacco, and managing cholesterol through lifestyle changes and medications. Many aneurysms remain asymptomatic until they grow large or rupture, but unruptured ones may cause localized symptoms such as pain behind the eye, vision disturbances, or numbness if pressing on nearby nerves. Rupture typically presents as a sudden, severe headache (often described as the "worst of one's life" for brain aneurysms), abdominal or back pain, nausea, dizziness, or loss of consciousness, constituting a medical emergency. Complications from rupture include subarachnoid hemorrhage, stroke, organ damage, or death, with survival rates varying by location and promptness of intervention. Diagnosis involves imaging techniques like CT angiography, MRI, or cerebral angiography to visualize the aneurysm's size and shape, often prompted by screening in high-risk individuals. Treatment for unruptured aneurysms may include watchful waiting with regular monitoring, while ruptured or high-risk cases require urgent intervention such as surgical clipping, endovascular coiling, or stent placement to reinforce the vessel wall. Prognosis improves with early detection, though long-term management often involves medications to control blood pressure and lifestyle modifications to reduce recurrence risk.
